title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: When Princess Mary heard from Nicholas that her brother was with the Rostovs at Yaroslavl, she prepared at once to go there, despite her aunt's efforts to talk her out of it. She meant not only to go herself but to take her nephew with her. She did not ask whether it would be hard or easy, possible or impossible, and did not want to know. It was her duty not only to be near her brother, who might be dying, but to do everything she could to bring his son to him, so she got ready to leave. She put down the fact that she had not heard from Prince Andrew himself to his being too weak to write, or to his thinking the long journey too hard and too dangerous for her and his son.

Within a few days Princess Mary was ready to start. She traveled in the huge family coach that had taken her to Voronezh, with a half-open trap and a baggage cart following. With her traveled Mademoiselle Bourienne, little Nicholas and his tutor, her old nurse, three maids, Tikhon, and a young footman and courier whom her aunt had sent along with her.

Going the usual way, through Moscow, was out of the question. The roundabout road she had to take, through Lipetsk, Ryazan, Vladimir and Shuya, was very long. Post horses were not to be had everywhere, so it was also very difficult, and near Ryazan, where the French were said to have shown themselves, it was even dangerous.

During this difficult journey Mademoiselle Bourienne, Dessalles and Princess Mary's servants were amazed at her energy and strength of spirit. She stayed up later and rose earlier than any of them, and no difficulty put her off. Her activity and energy rubbed off on her fellow travelers, and by the end of the second week they were nearing Yaroslavl.

She had spent her last days in Voronezh in the happiest time of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or unsettled her. It filled her whole soul, it had become part of her, and she no longer fought against it. Lately she had become convinced that she loved and was loved, though she never spelled this out to herself in words. The conviction had come at her last meeting with Nicholas, when he came to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Nicholas had not said a single word about the possibility that Prince Andrew's relations with Natasha might be renewed if he recovered, but Princess Mary saw from his face that he knew it and thought about it.

Yet even so, he treated her just as before — considerately, delicately, lovingly. Sometimes it even seemed to Princess Mary that he was glad the family connection between them allowed him to show his friendship more freely. She knew she was loving for the first and only time in her life, and she felt that she was loved, and she was happy about it.

But the happiness in one part of her soul did not stop her from feeling her grief for her brother with full force. On the contrary, the peace she had found there made it easier to let her feeling for her brother run free. At the moment she left Voronezh it was so strong that the people seeing her off took one look at her careworn, despairing face and felt sure she would fall ill on the way. But the very difficulties and worries of the journey, which she took in hand so actively, saved her for a time from her grief and gave her strength.

As always happens on a journey, Princess Mary thought only of the traveling itself and forgot where it led. But as she drew near Yaroslavl, the thought of what might be waiting for her there came back — and not after many days, but that very evening. Her agitation rose to its highest pitch.

The courier had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and how Prince Andrew was. He met the big coach just as it was entering the town gates, and he was appalled by the terrible pallor of the princess's face looking out at him from the window.
"I've found out everything, Your Excellency: the Rostovs are staying at the merchant Bronnikov's house, in the Square not far from here, right above the Volga," said the courier.

Princess Mary looked at him with frightened inquiry. She did not understand why he had not answered what she most wanted to know: how was her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked that question for her.
"How is the prince?" she asked.
"His Excellency is staying in the same house with them."
"Then he is alive," thought Princess Mary, and she asked in a low voice, "How is he?"
"The servants say he is still the same."

Princess Mary did not ask what "still the same" might mean. With an unnoticed glance at little seven-year-old Nicholas, who sat in front of her looking at the town with pleasure, she bowed her head and did not raise it again until the heavy coach, rumbling, shaking and swaying, came to a stop. The carriage steps clattered as they were let down.

The carriage door opened. On the left there was water — a great river — and on the right a porch. There were people at the entrance: servants, and a rosy girl with a large plait of black hair, who smiled in a way that struck Princess Mary as unpleasantly affected. (This was Sonya.) Princess Mary ran up the steps. "This way, this way!" said the girl, with the same artificial smile, and the princess found herself in the hall facing an elderly woman of Oriental type, who came quickly toward her with a look of emotion. This was the countess. She embraced Princess Mary and kissed her.
"Mon enfant!" she murmured, "je vous aime et vous connais depuis longtemps." *
* "My child! I love you and have known you a long time."

Despite her agitation, Princess Mary realized that this was the countess and that she had to say something to her. Hardly knowing how she did it, she managed to utter a few polite phrases in French, in the same tone as those that had been addressed to her, and asked, "How is he?"
"The doctor says he is not in danger," said the countess, but as she spoke she raised her eyes with a sigh, and the gesture contradicted her words.
"Where is he? Can I see him — can I?" asked the princess.

"One moment, Princess, one moment, my dear! Is this his son?" said the countess, turning to little Nicholas, who was coming in with Dessalles. "There will be room for everybody, it's a big house. Oh, what a lovely boy!"

The countess took Princess Mary into the drawing room, where Sonya was talking to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy, and the old count came in and welcomed the princess. He had changed very much since Princess Mary had last seen him. Then he had been a brisk, cheerful, self-assured old man. Now he seemed a pitiful, bewildered one. While he talked to Princess Mary he kept looking around as if asking everyone whether he was doing the right thing. After the destruction of Moscow and of his property, thrown out of his accustomed groove, he seemed to have lost the sense of his own importance and to feel that there was no longer a place for him in life.

She had only one desire, to see her brother as soon as possible, and she was vexed that at the very moment when that was all she wanted, they were trying to entertain her and pretending to admire her nephew. Even so, the princess noticed everything going on around her and felt she had to submit, for a time, to this new order of things she had entered. She knew it was necessary, and though it was hard for her she was not angry with these people.
"This is my niece," said the count, introducing Sonya. "You don't know her, Princess?"

Princess Mary turned to Sonya and, trying to stifle the hostile feeling that rose in her toward the girl, she kissed her. But it weighed on her that everyone around her was in a mood so far from what filled her own heart.
"Where is he?" she asked again, addressing them all.
"He is downstairs. Natasha is with him," answered Sonya, blushing. "We've sent to ask. I think you must be tired, Princess."

Tears of vexation came into Princess Mary's eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to get to him, when light, impetuous and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door. The princess looked round and saw Natasha come in, almost running — the same Natasha she had liked so little when they met in Moscow long ago.

But hardly had the princess looked at Natasha's face when she realized that here was a true companion in her grief, and therefore a friend. She ran to meet her, embraced her and began to cry on her shoulder.

As soon as Natasha, sitting at the head of Prince Andrew's bed, heard of Princess Mary's arrival, she softly left his room and hurried to her with those swift steps that had sounded buoyant to Princess Mary.

Her agitated face had only one expression when she ran into the drawing room: love — boundless love for him, for Mary, and for everything that was close to the man she loved; and pity, suffering for others, and a passionate desire to give herself entirely to helping them. It was plain that at that moment Natasha had no thought in her heart of herself or of her own relations with Prince Andrew.
Princess Mary, with her acute sensibility, understood all this at the first glance at Natasha's face, and wept on her shoulder with sorrowful pleasure.
"Come, come to him, Mary," said Natasha, leading her into the other room.
Princess Mary raised her head, dried her eyes and turned to Natasha. She felt that from her she would be able to understand and learn everything.
"How..." she began her question but stopped short.
She felt that it was impossible to ask or to answer in words. Natasha's face and eyes would have to tell her everything, more clearly and more deeply.

Natasha was looking at her, but seemed afraid and unsure whether to say all she knew. She seemed to feel that before those luminous eyes, which penetrated into the very depths of her heart, it was impossible not to tell the whole truth she saw. And suddenly Natasha's lips twitched, ugly wrinkles gathered around her mouth, and covering her face with her hands she burst into sobs.
Princess Mary understood.
Still, she hoped, and she asked in words she herself did not trust:
"But how is his wound? What is his general condition?"
"You, you... will see," was all Natasha could say.
They sat for a little while downstairs near his room until they had stopped crying and could go to him with calm faces.
"How has his whole illness gone? Did he get worse long ago? When did this happen?" Princess Mary asked.

Natasha told her that at first his fever and pain had put him in danger, but at Troitsa that had passed, and the doctor had only feared gangrene. That danger had passed too. When they reached Yaroslavl the wound had begun to fester (Natasha knew all about such things as festering), and the doctor had said that the festering might take a normal course. Then a fever set in, but the doctor had said the fever was not very serious.
"But two days ago this suddenly happened," said Natasha, struggling with her sobs. "I don't know why, but you will see what he is like."
"Is he weaker? Thinner?" asked the princess.
"No, it's not that, but worse. You will see. Oh, Mary, he is too good, he cannot, cannot live, because..."
